subject: Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model

messages.author: 9f2f778ca0b4e8e1
messages.subject: Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model
parts:
So, Stan is awesome. It's fast enough that it's making my current study, which entails fitting models of intertemporal choice to human subjects in real time, possible. Hooray!

Currently, I'm having trouble getting my chains to converge consistently. This goes for several models, but let's at least begin by considering a model that in general works fine but for a particular dataset has trouble converging in one of the parameters. Load the attached R source (the Stan code is a string literal) and try something like:

m = stan_model(model_code = code)
fit = sampling(m, data = dat, chains = 7)
summary(fit)$summary[c("v30", "scurve", "rho"), "Rhat"]

As a rule, the Rhat for rho will be above 1.1, typically at 1.5 or 2.0. Tweaking iter, warmup, thin, or init doesn't seem to help.

I can get convergence if I restrict the support of rho to [0, .11] or [.1, 1] (and set iter to something big), but not, e.g., [.01, .99]. Looking at plots, I would guess that the lumpiness of rho's marginal density is to blame. But I don't know what to do about it.

(The reason why the supports of v30 and scurve aren't [0, 1], if you're wondering, is to avoid floating-point overflows leading to NaNs. Formerly, I had a fancier way around this where I switched to a logarithmic approximation (heavily abusing Stan's step() to compensate for the lack of conditional expressions with real numbers), but then I began getting error message about Stan not being able to find a small enough step size.)

That sounds like you indeed have a "lumpy" (aka multimodal) posterior.

> (The reason why the supports of v30 and scurve aren't [0, 1], if you're wondering, is to avoid floating-point overflows
> leading to NaNs. Formerly, I had a fancier way around this where I switched to a logarithmic approximation (heavily
> abusing Stan's step() to compensate for the lack of conditional expressions with real numbers), but then I began getting
> error message about Stan not being able to find a small enough step size.)

You should think of this as a warning about your parameterization,
too. If it's going off the rails, it probably indicates something's
wrong with the parameterization of the model.

Abstracting away from the transforms whose motivation I don't understand,
you have a linear predictor for a logistic regression that looks like:

a * (x1 * pow(1 + b * x2, c)
- x2 * pow(1 + d * x3, c));

a, b, c, and d are parameters and x1, x2, x3, and x4 are
(positive) data. (I pasted in the full model below.)

Did you look at trace plots and find stable chains around
different modes? If you initialize the chains near a solution
do they stay near where they're initialized, or do they wander?

You might want to try simplifying the parameterization.
For a start, why not characterize parameter a directy instead of
in terms of scurve, curve and e?

Also, I don't understand why you'd write something like this:

parameters {
...
real <lower = 0, upper = 1> rho;
...
transformed parameters {
real rho_v;
rho_v <- 10 * rho;
}


Why not just declare rho_v directly as a parameter
using:

real<lower=0, upper=10> rho_v;

It can also help to regularize the data.

You could move any of the transformed parameters you don't
care about reporting to be local variables in the model.

- Bob

P.S. Here's the model for reference:

----------------------
code = 'data
{int <lower = 0> N_ts;
vector<lower = 0>[N_ts] ssr;
vector<lower = 0>[N_ts] ssd;
vector<lower = 0>[N_ts] llr;
vector<lower = 0>[N_ts] lld;
int <lower = 0, upper = 1> choose_ll[N_ts];}
parameters
{real <lower = .0005, upper = 1 - 1e-12> v30;
real <lower = 1e-12, upper = .9> scurve;
real <lower = 0, upper = 1> rho;}
transformed parameters
{vector[N_ts] choose_ll_p_logit;
real curve; real e; real a; real rho_v;
curve <- 10/(1 - scurve) - 10;
e <- 1/-curve;
a <- (1/pow(v30, curve) - 1)/30;
rho_v <- 10 * rho;
for (t in 1 : N_ts)
choose_ll_p_logit[t] <- rho_v *
(llr[t] * pow(1 + a * lld[t], e) -
ssr[t] * pow(1 + a * ssd[t], e));}
model
{choose_ll ~ bernoulli_logit(choose_ll_p_logit);}'
------------------------

messages.author: 9f2f778ca0b4e8e1
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model
parts:
On Monday, November 12, 2012 3:14:43 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
You might want to try simplifying the parameterization.
For a start, why not characterize parameter a directy instead of
in terms of scurve, curve and e?

My motivation behind the hairy parametrization is basically to keep the parameters interpretable. As the model is now, v30 is the discounted value of a reward at 30 days (so if v30 = .6, the subject would be indifferent between receiving $100 today and receiving $60 in 30 days), scurve controls how flat the discounting curve is (such that scurve = 0 makes an exponential curve, scurve = 1 makes a curve that is almost everywhere a horizontal line, and the transition between the two bounds "feels" linear given graphs on human scales), and rho controls how sensitive the subject is to differences between options (such that when rho = 0, the subject chooses completely at random, and when rho = 1, the subject is practically deterministic). Of course, I could compute marginal densities of such quantities regardless of the parameterization. The problem with parameters that are hard to interpret, as I see it, is that the priors are then really hard to interpret. And even though I don't want genuinely informative priors in this case, since I'm comparing models and the setting is the lab instead of the real world, I still have to worry about issues like the scale of the priors. For example, under one, more natural parameterization for this model, curvature of the discounting function varies such that a range of curvatures with large differences for behavior have the same prior mass as a range of curvatures with small differences for behavior. In effect, the latter range would be favored, although this is undesirable. Is there a nicer way around this sort of problem than using interpretable parameters?
 
As for putting rho in [0, 1] instead of [0, 10], that's just because 1 is a rounder number than 10.
It can also help to regularize the data.

Rescaling the time values (ssd and lld) would change the meaning of v30, but rescaling the reward values (ssr and ssd) has, to my surprise, solved the problem, at least in this case. The chains converge fine now. Thanks! I'll see how far rescaling can take me. (And now that I think about it, perhaps I could keep the meaning of v30 for rescaled time values if I altered the calculation of a appropriately.)

You could move any of the transformed parameters you don't
care about reporting to be local variables in the model.
Good point, I'm not sure why I didn't do that to begin with.

One reason this can happen is that all the chains might be more
likely to start in the region of the same mode. If that happens,
it can appear like convergence when you're not really exploring
the entire posterior. In some cases, this can be OK if you know
there's only one reasonable mode and know where to look for it,
or if there are several equivalent modes in a non-identifiable model.

Did you ever check the traceplots to see what was going on in cases
that didn't converge?

- Bob

parts: On Wednesday, November 14, 2012 2:13:49 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

On 11/13/12 8:33 PM, Kodi Arfer wrote:
My motivation behind the hairy parametrization is basically to keep the parameters interpretable.

Looking at it, I figured it was something like this.

The alternative is to keep the data/parameters on a regularized
scale and then compute generated_quantities that are interpretable
by scaling.  This helps rather than hurts for specifying "default"
priors.  (In general, whatever priors you use, you should check sensitivity
to prior assumptions.)

It helps? That's counterintuitive to me. Is the idea that I would look at the densities of the generated quantities in order to decide how to set the parameter priors? I guess that makes sense. The usual sort of prior-checking, in which you look at the inferences the model would make with your real data, is not really possible for my study because the model is being fit and decisions based upon the analysis (decisions of what choice to offer the subject) are being made in real time, during the experiment. But I can at least examine the prior marginal densities of generated quantities.
Rescaling the time values (ssd and lld) would change the meaning of v30, but rescaling the reward values (ssr and ssd) has, to my surprise, solved the problem, at least in this case.

One reason this can happen is that all the chains might be more
likely to start in the region of the same mode.
Or, I now realize, it may just be because shrinking the reward values is equivalent to shrinking the support of rho.

Did you ever check the traceplots to see what was going on in cases
that didn't converge?

I did. The trend seems to be that the chains spend most of their time around rho = .1 (although the posterior mode has a rho of about .59) and sometimes wander off. For example, here I run three chains starting from the mode:

> fit = sampling(m, data = dat, iter = 20000, thin = 5, chains = 3, refresh = -1, init = rep(list(list(v30 = 0.09263812, scurve = 0.07991578, rho = 0.5909527)), 3))
> summary(fit)$summary[c("v30", "scurve", "rho"),"Rhat"]

v30   scurve      rho
1.052642 1.029246 1.782057

http://i.imgur.com/RmoBV.png

I've noticed that setting warmup to a low value gets the chains to explore the whole range of rho:

> fit = sampling(m, data = dat, iter = 20000, warmup = 20, thin = 5, chains = 3, refresh = -1, init = rep(list(list(v30 = 0.09263812, scurve = 0.07991578, rho = 0.5909527)), 3))
> summary(fit)$summary[c("v30", "scurve", "rho"),"Rhat"]

v30   scurve      rho
1.004355 1.005207 1.001610

http://i.imgur.com/Jr5Z0.png

Now I can see that the posterior distribution of rho is in fact unimodal: http://i.imgur.com/pySru.png

But that figure doesn't match a density plot of rho from the same fit object: http://i.imgur.com/u4OG7.png

It depends how strict a "Bayesian" you want to be. If you
choose a default prior for a regression prior then normalize
predictors, the prior's technically derived from the data rather
than properly "prior".

> Is the idea that I would look at the densities of the generated quantities in
> order to decide how to set the parameter priors? I guess that makes sense.

It's at least obvious that even if you have strong prior information,
if it's for a coefficient for height, then rescaling height from
inches to cm should rescale the prior.

> The usual sort of prior-checking, in which
> you look at the inferences the model would make with your real data, is not really possible for my study because the
> model is being fit and decisions based upon the analysis (decisions of what choice to offer the subject) are being made
> in real time, during the experiment. But I can at least examine the prior marginal densities of generated quantities.

Exactly. You want to see if they're dramatically affected by
the prior assumptions or insensitive to them.

> Rescaling the time values (ssd and lld) would change the meaning of v30, but rescaling the reward values (ssr
> and ssd) has, to my surprise, solved the problem, at least in this case.

> rho of about .59) and sometimes wander off.

That's possible in cases where there's not much data.
The mode of a beta can be pretty far from the mean
proportionally.

For example, here I run three chains starting from the mode:
>
> |
> > fit = sampling(m, data = dat, iter = 20000, thin = 5, chains = 3, refresh = -1, init = rep(list(list(v30 =
> 0.09263812, scurve = 0.07991578, rho = 0.5909527)), 3))
> > summary(fit)$summary[c("v30", "scurve", "rho"),"Rhat"]
> v30 scurve rho
> 1.052642 1.029246 1.782057
> |
>
> http://i.imgur.com/RmoBV.png

>
> |
> > fit = sampling(m, data = dat, iter = 20000, warmup = 20, thin = 5, chains = 3, refresh = -1, init = rep(list(list(v30
> = 0.09263812, scurve = 0.07991578, rho = 0.5909527)), 3))
> > summary(fit)$summary[c("v30", "scurve", "rho"),"Rhat"]
> v30 scurve rho
> 1.004355 1.005207 1.001610

I wouldn't trust this option. It doesn't give the sampler much
time to adapt step sizes. You could instead try what happens by hand-tuning
various step sizes rather than letting adaptation do it.

> http://i.imgur.com/Jr5Z0.png
>
> Now I can see that the posterior distribution of rho is in fact unimodal: http://i.imgur.com/pySru.png

Why not fit the density in one dimension for just rho?
In R, if samples are the samples extracted from the fit,
then :

> plot(density(samples$rho))

Or just use a histogram:

> histogram(samples$rho)

I find plotting vs. lp__ confuses the issue of the
modality of p(rho|data)
> But that figure doesn't match a density plot of rho from the same fit object: http://i.imgur.com/u4OG7.png

A programming bug perhaps?

- Bob
